subject: nlp
title: Practice bank: Lecture 9 (Scaling NLP)
description: New practice questions on Lecture 9 (induction heads, scaling laws, mixture of experts, modularity, distillation and data poisoning), with scaling-law and distillation calculations, plus mechanistic interpretability from the tutorial. Written for exam revision from the slides. Not from the lecturer: the answers are unofficial.
negativeMarkingNote: The real Moodle quiz uses negative marking on MCQ questions: picking all right and wrong answers on a question results in a mark of 0.

questions.question: What is the "phase change" associated with induction heads (Lecture 9)?
choices: With scale, the model realises the task cannot be done by learning alone and switches to using the context (in-context learning)
The model's loss suddenly increases at the end of training
Attention heads switch from the encoder to the decoder
The model switches from greedy decoding to beam search
questions.explanation: Slide 2. Induction heads tend to emerge with scale and are argued to be the mechanism for most in-context learning (slide 3).

questions.question: True or False: An induction head needs two attention layers working together: a previous-token head and a head that uses it to copy what followed an earlier occurrence of the current token.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: The circuit on slide 2 shows a "previous token head" feeding the induction head. The lecturer linked this to stacked layers in L5 and to the project.

questions.question:
The Kaplan et al. fits on slide 4 are $L(N) = (N / 8.8 \times 10^{13})^{-0.076}$ (parameters) and $L(D) = (D / 5.4 \times 10^{13})^{-0.095}$ (tokens).
(a) $L$ for a model with $N = 10^9$ parameters.
(b) The factor by which $L$ is multiplied when $N$ grows 10×.
(c) $L$ for $D = 10^{10}$ tokens.
(d) The factor when $D$ grows 10×.
questions.explanation: A power law is a straight line on log–log axes: each 10× in scale gives the same fractional improvement, which is what makes the improvements predictable.

questions.question: Which statements about neural scaling laws are made on the slides?
choices: Language-model loss improves smoothly and predictably as compute, data and parameters grow
Each factor has a power-law relationship with the loss when not bottlenecked by the others
The regularity is believed to be due to the Zipf distribution of language
Scaling up removes the need for more data
questions.explanation: Slide 4 (Kaplan et al.). The three must be scaled in tandem.

questions.question: In a sparsely-gated mixture-of-experts layer:
choices: A gating network selects a few experts for each input, so only part of the parameters is used per token
Every expert processes every token and the outputs are averaged
Experts are separate models trained on different languages
The gate is fixed by hand
questions.explanation: Slide 5 (Shazeer et al.): the gate picks two experts here. Sparsity gives the capacity of a large model at the compute cost of a small one.

questions.question: An MoE layer has 64 experts, each with 4.2M parameters, and the gate selects the top 2 experts per token. (a) What fraction of the expert parameters is used for one token? (b) How many expert parameters are stored? (c) How many are used per token?
In Recurrent Independent Mechanisms (RIMs), what role does attention play?
choices: It guides information flow through whole network modules, so only the relevant modules are activated and they communicate sparsely
It replaces the recurrence entirely
It masks future tokens
It is used only to read the output
questions.explanation: Slide 6: modularity and sparsity baked in; modules compete via input attention and communicate sparsely.

questions.question: True or False: Lecture 9 presents sparsity (mixture of experts) and modularity (e.g. RIMs) as ways to get emergent abilities without needing as much scale.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: The slides' heading is "Emergence without the scale".

questions.question:
A teacher network gives logits $(4,2,1,0)$ for four classes; the true label is class 1.
(a) The teacher's probability for class 2 at temperature 1.
(b) The same at temperature 4 (softened labels for distillation).
(c) The hard label's probability for class 2.
questions.solution: (a) $\text{softmax}(4,2,1,0)_2 = 0.1125$. (b) Dividing by 4: $(1, 0.5, 0.25, 0)$, $p_2 = 0.2479$. (c) The one-hot label gives 0.
questions.explanation: Distillation trains the student on the teacher's soft labels, which say how similar the wrong classes are to the right one: "far more detailed labels" than one-hot targets (slide 7). The temperature is the same knob as in L5.

questions.question: Which statements about knowledge distillation are true?
choices: A big (teacher) network is used to train a smaller (student) network
The student learns from the teacher's soft predictions, which carry more detail than hard labels
The student can also be trained on the true labels at the same time
The student must be larger than the teacher
questions.explanation: The slide shows soft labels from the teacher and hard labels from the data both feeding the student.

questions.question: The data-poisoning slides describe how model-generated data filtering back into training causes collapse. Which statements match them?
choices: Probable events are over-estimated and improbable events under-estimated
Errors come from finite sampling and approximate fitting
The tails of the distribution shrink over time
Collapse takes thousands of generations to appear
questions.explanation: It can happen "over a handful of generations".

questions.question: What is the high-level goal of mechanistic interpretability (Tutorial 8.1)?
choices: To reverse-engineer the computations inside a trained network into human-understandable mechanisms (circuits), such as induction heads
To make models smaller by pruning
To measure a model's accuracy on benchmarks
To write programs that generate neural networks
questions.explanation: Not on the slides: this follows the standard definition used in the tutorial. Induction heads are a classic example of a circuit found this way.

questions.question: True or False: Probing a representation with a classifier shows that information is present, while mechanistic interpretability tries to show how the network actually uses it.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Probing is correlational ("decodable"); mechanistic work traces the causal circuit (e.g. which heads compose into an induction head). Tutorial 8.1 topic; standard definitions.
